<reflection>
The first experiment provided NLL values for all 20 models. The top models (M6 and M8) have the lowest NLL, but many others are within a very narrow range (differences < 0.04). This indicates that with only one dataset, most models fit the data almost equally well, and no mechanism can be confidently ruled out except possibly M5 (which has a much higher NLL). The aim of the first experiment was to establish a baseline, and it succeeded in showing that discrimination requires additional data. The challenge now is to design a second experiment that amplifies differences across the entire set of plausible mechanisms, not just between the top two.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the many similar models, we need to probe different kinetic regimes. The proposed experiment uses a higher catalyst concentration (0.1 M) to stress dimerization and deactivation pathways that depend on catalyst concentration. Adding initial product (0.2 M) tests reversibility and product-induced inhibition or deactivation. A higher substrate concentration (2.0 M) ensures that substrate is not limiting initially, making the rate more sensitive to catalyst-related effects. This combination is likely to produce progress curves that differ significantly between mechanisms involving dimerization (e.g., M2, M3), deactivation (e.g., M9–M20), and reversible activation (e.g., M6, M8). By moving away from the first experiment's conditions, we avoid repeating similar regimes and aim to reveal distinct functional forms in the rate laws.
</hypothesis>
